subtasks.testStrategy: Deploy the function to a development environment. Manually update the status of a document in the `consultation_requests` collection in the Firestore console. Check the function logs to ensure it was triggered correctly and monitor the test device to confirm the push notification is received.

tasks.title: Write Unit Tests for Critical Functions
tasks.description: Write a suite of unit tests for existing critical business logic, focusing on services, formatters, and validators to improve code reliability.
tasks.details:
Using the Jest framework set up in Task 4, create test files for the following: 
- `firebaseService.js`: Mock Firebase functions using `jest.mock` to test data fetching, vehicle registration, and consultation request logic without making actual API calls. 
- **Validators**: Test input validation functions for forms (e.g., email format, password strength, vehicle year). Test with both valid and invalid inputs. 
- **Formatters**: Test utility functions that format data for display (e.g., currency formatters for price, date formatters for timestamps).
tasks.testStrategy: 1. Run all tests via `npm test` and ensure they pass. 2. Integrate a code coverage tool like `jest --coverage` to measure test effectiveness. Aim for an initial coverage of over 70% for the targeted files. 3. Ensure tests are run as part of the pre-commit hook.

subtasks.title: Create Test Setup for firebaseService.js with Firebase Mocks
subtasks.description: Create a `firebaseService.test.js` file and implement the necessary mocks for the `@react-native-firebase/firestore` module using `jest.mock`. This foundational step will prevent actual database calls during tests.
subtasks.details:
In the new `__tests__/services/firebaseService.test.js` file, use `jest.mock('@react-native-firebase/firestore', () => { ... })` to return a mock implementation. The mock should allow for spying on and controlling the behavior of functions like `collection`, `doc`, `get`, and `add` for subsequent tests.
<info added on 2025-11-27T14:05:30.443Z>
Global mocks have been configured in `jest.setup.js`, centralizing the setup for all tests. This includes mocks for Firebase messaging, functions, and crashlytics. A mock for `PermissionsAndroid` has also been added to support testing for Android 13+ permissions.
</info added on 2025-11-27T14:05:30.443Z>
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify that running `npm test` does not result in errors related to the firebaseService test file and that no actual network requests to Firebase are made.

subtasks.title: Write Unit Tests for Data Fetching Functions in firebaseService.js
subtasks.description: Using the mock setup from the previous task, write unit tests for the data retrieval functions in `firebaseService.js`, specifically `getVehicles` and `getUserProfile`. Tests should cover both successful and empty/failed responses.
subtasks.details: For `getVehicles`, mock a successful response from `firestore().collection('vehicles').get()` and assert that the function correctly maps and returns the documents. For `getUserProfile`, test the case where a document is found and the case where it isn't, ensuring it returns user data or null accordingly.
subtasks.testStrategy: Run tests and assert that the functions return the expected data structures based on the mocked Firestore responses. Ensure tests pass for both success and failure scenarios.

subtasks.title: Write Unit Tests for Data Writing Functions in firebaseService.js
subtasks.description: Write unit tests for the functions that perform write operations, such as `registerVehicle` and `createConsultationRequest`. The tests should verify that the correct data payload is passed to the mocked Firestore functions.
subtasks.details: For each write function, create a test that calls the function with sample data. Use `expect(mockedAddFunction).toHaveBeenCalledWith(...)` to assert that the mocked Firestore `add` method was called with the exact object structure expected.
subtasks.testStrategy: Confirm that tests pass and that the spy on the mocked `add` function correctly captures the function calls with the appropriate arguments.

subtasks.title: Implement Unit Tests for Validator and Formatter Utilities
subtasks.description: Create test files for `validators.js` and `formatters.js`. Write a comprehensive suite of tests covering all functions with both valid and invalid inputs to ensure they behave as expected across various edge cases.
subtasks.details: Create `__tests__/utils/validators.test.js` and `__tests__/utils/formatters.test.js`. For validators (e.g., `isValidEmail`, `isStrongPassword`), test with multiple valid and invalid strings. For formatters (e.g., `formatCurrency`, `formatDate`), test with numbers, valid timestamp objects, and null/undefined inputs to ensure robust formatting.
subtasks.testStrategy: Execute the tests and verify that all assertions pass. Check that each function's output matches the expected result for a wide range of inputs, including edge cases.

subtasks.title: Run Test Suite and Generate Code Coverage Report
subtasks.description: Execute the entire test suite and use Jest's built-in coverage tool to generate a report. Analyze the report to ensure the newly tested files meet the project's target coverage of over 70%.
subtasks.details: Run the command `npm test -- --coverage` in the terminal. This will execute all tests and create a `coverage/` directory. Open the `lcov-report/index.html` file in a browser to review the statement, branch, and function coverage for the targeted files. If coverage is below 70%, add tests for any missed logic.
subtasks.testStrategy: Confirm that the coverage command runs successfully and produces a report. Verify that the coverage percentages for `firebaseService.js`, `validators.js`, and `formatters.js` are at or above the 70% threshold.

tasks.title: Enhance Admin Management Features
tasks.description: Implement high-priority admin features, including emergency vehicle deletion and a user management interface for suspending or activating accounts.
tasks.details: 1. **Emergency Delete**: In the admin panel's vehicle view, add a 'Delete' button. On click, it should trigger a Firebase Function that performs a hard delete of the vehicle document and its associated images in Firebase Storage. This action should be logged in an admin activity log collection. 2. **User Management**: Create a new screen in the admin panel to list all users. Implement functionality to search and filter users. Each user item should have a toggle/button to change a `status` field in their user document (e.g., from 'active' to 'suspended'). Firestore security rules must be updated to deny writes from suspended users.
tasks.testStrategy: 1. As an admin, delete a test vehicle and verify its document and storage files are removed. 2. As an admin, suspend a test user account. Log in as the suspended user and verify they are blocked from performing key actions (e.g., creating a consultation). 3. Verify all admin actions are correctly recorded in the activity log.

subtasks.title: Create Firebase Function for Emergency Vehicle Deletion
subtasks.description: Develop and deploy an HTTPS callable Firebase Function that hard-deletes a specified vehicle document from Firestore, removes its associated images from Firebase Storage, and logs the action in an 'admin_activity_log' collection.
subtasks.details: The function should accept a `vehicleId` as input. It must first authenticate the request to ensure the caller is an admin. It will then fetch the vehicle document to get image URLs, delete files from the default storage bucket, delete the Firestore document, and finally create a log entry with admin UID, target vehicleId, and timestamp.
subtasks.testStrategy: Use the Firebase Local Emulator Suite to invoke the function with a test vehicle ID. Verify that the Firestore document is deleted, the corresponding files in the Storage emulator are removed, and a log entry is created. Test unauthorized access to ensure it fails.

subtasks.title: Implement 'Delete Vehicle' Button in Admin Panel UI
subtasks.description: In the admin's vehicle management screen, add a 'Delete' button to each vehicle entry. This button will trigger a confirmation modal and, upon confirmation, call the vehicle deletion Firebase Function.
subtasks.details: Locate the component responsible for rendering the list of vehicles for admins. Add a styled 'Delete' button. Implement an `Alert` or a custom modal to confirm the deletion. On confirmation, use the Firebase Functions SDK to call the `deleteVehicle` function, passing the `vehicleId`.
subtasks.testStrategy: As an admin, navigate to the vehicle list. Press the delete button for a test vehicle. Verify the confirmation modal appears. Confirm deletion and check the UI for the vehicle's removal. Check Firestore and Storage to confirm deletion via the function.

subtasks.title: Build User Management Screen UI
subtasks.description: Create a new screen in the admin panel to display a list of all application users. The screen should include a search bar to find users by email or name.
subtasks.details: Create a new screen component, e.g., `UserManagementScreen.js`. Add it to the admin navigation stack. Fetch all documents from the 'users' collection and display them in a `FlatList`. Each list item should show key user details (name, email, status). Implement a search input that filters the displayed list client-side or by re-querying Firestore.
subtasks.testStrategy: Navigate to the new admin screen and verify that all registered users are listed correctly. Test the search functionality by typing a known user's name or email and confirm the list filters as expected. Ensure the UI is responsive.

subtasks.title: Implement User Account Suspend/Activate Functionality
subtasks.description: In the User Management screen, add a toggle switch or button to each user item that allows an admin to change the user's status between 'active' and 'suspended'.
subtasks.details: For each user in the list, add a `Switch` or `Button` component that reflects the user's current `status` from Firestore. When the admin interacts with the control, it should trigger a Firestore update operation to change the `status` field on the corresponding user document. The UI should optimistically update or refetch data to show the new status.
subtasks.testStrategy: As an admin, go to the user management screen. Change the status of a test user from 'active' to 'suspended' and back. Verify the change is reflected in the UI and in the user's document in the Firestore console. Also log this admin action.

subtasks.title: Update Firestore Security Rules to Restrict Suspended Users
subtasks.description: Modify `firestore.rules` to deny write access to key collections (e.g., 'consultation_requests', 'vehicles') for users whose `status` field in their own user document is set to 'suspended'.
subtasks.details: Edit the `firestore.rules` file. For relevant collections, update the `allow write` conditions to include a check against the requesting user's document. The rule should look something like: `allow create: if request.auth != null && get(/databases/$(database)/documents/users/$(request.auth.uid)).data.status == 'active';`
subtasks.testStrategy: Using the Firestore Rules Emulator, write unit tests for a suspended user attempting to create a document in a protected collection. The test should assert that the write operation is denied. Manually log in to the app as a suspended test user and attempt a write action to confirm it is blocked.

tasks.title: Implement Advanced Vehicle Search and Filters
tasks.description: Develop an advanced search interface allowing users to filter and sort the vehicle list by multiple criteria such as price range, year, and manufacturer.
tasks.details: 1. Create a 'Filter' modal or screen accessible from the main vehicle list. 2. Add UI components for filtering: sliders for price/year range, multi-select pickers for manufacturers. 3. When the user applies filters, construct a composite Firestore query. For example: `firestore().collection('vehicles').where('price', '>=', minPrice).where('price', '<=', maxPrice).orderBy('price').limit(20)`. Note Firestore's limitations on composite queries may require data duplication or a more advanced search solution like Algolia if complexity increases. 4. Implement sorting options (e.g., Price: Low to High) which will modify the `orderBy()` clause of the Firestore query.
tasks.testStrategy: 1. Unit test the query construction logic. 2. Manually test the UI by applying various filter combinations and verifying that the returned vehicle list is accurate. 3. Test edge cases, such as a filter combination that yields no results, ensuring a user-friendly message is displayed.

subtasks.title: Create Filter Modal UI and Navigation Trigger
subtasks.description: Create a new modal component for the advanced search filters and add a 'Filter' button to the main vehicle list screen to open it.
subtasks.details: In the `VehicleListScreen.tsx`, add a new `Button` or `TouchableOpacity` component that, when pressed, will present the `FilterModal`. The `FilterModal` component should be created as a new file, e.g., `src/components/modals/FilterModal.tsx`. Initially, it can be a simple shell with a title, a close button, and an 'Apply Filters' button.
subtasks.testStrategy: Manually press the 'Filter' button on the vehicle list screen and verify that the modal appears correctly and can be dismissed. Snapshot testing can be used for the initial modal layout.

subtasks.title: Develop UI Components for Filtering Criteria
subtasks.description: Implement the UI components inside the filter modal for price range, year range, and manufacturer selection.
subtasks.details: Inside `FilterModal.tsx`, add the necessary UI controls. Use a slider component (e.g., from `@react-native-community/slider`) for price and year ranges. For manufacturers, implement a multi-select list. Fetch the list of unique manufacturers from the Firestore 'vehicles' collection once. Use `useState` within the modal to manage the temporary state of these inputs before they are applied.
subtasks.testStrategy: Render the modal component in a storybook or test environment. Interact with the sliders and the multi-select component to ensure their state is updated correctly within the component. Verify the UI is responsive and user-friendly.

subtasks.title: Implement Filter State Management
subtasks.description: Establish a mechanism, likely using React Context or a global state manager, to hold the applied filter values and make them accessible to the vehicle list screen.
subtasks.details: Create a `FilterContext` to manage the state of active filters. The context provider should wrap the main navigator or at least the `VehicleListScreen`. The `FilterModal` will use the context's updater function when the 'Apply Filters' button is pressed. The `VehicleListScreen` will consume this context to get the current filter criteria.
subtasks.testStrategy: Unit test the context provider and consumer. Create a test component that updates the filter context and another that reads from it, and assert that the values are passed correctly.

subtasks.title: Build Dynamic Firestore Query Construction Service
subtasks.description: Create a utility function or service that takes a filter object and dynamically constructs a Firestore query with the appropriate 'where' and 'orderBy' clauses.
subtasks.details: Create a new file, e.g., `src/services/firestoreQueryBuilder.ts`. This file will export a function `buildVehicleQuery(filters)` which accepts an object like `{ minPrice, maxPrice, manufacturers, sortBy }`. The function will start with `firestore().collection('vehicles')` and conditionally chain `.where()` and `.orderBy()` methods based on the provided filters. It must handle cases where filters are not set. Note Firestore's limitation: range filters can only be on one field per query.
subtasks.testStrategy: Write unit tests for the `buildVehicleQuery` function. Pass various filter combinations (including empty/null values) and assert that the generated Firestore query object has the correct structure and clauses. Mock the firestore object for these tests.

subtasks.title: Integrate Filtering Logic into Vehicle List Screen
subtasks.description: Connect the filter state and the query builder to the vehicle list screen to fetch and display the filtered and sorted data from Firestore.
subtasks.details: In `VehicleListScreen.tsx`, use the `FilterContext` to get the current filters. Use a `useEffect` hook that listens for changes to these filters. When filters change, call the `buildVehicleQuery` service with the new filter state, execute the resulting query against Firestore, and update the component's state with the new list of vehicles. Also, implement a loading indicator and a message for when no results are found.
subtasks.testStrategy: Perform end-to-end manual testing. Open the modal, apply various filter combinations (price, manufacturer, sort order), and verify that the vehicle list updates correctly. Test edge cases like clearing all filters and applying a filter that returns no results.

tasks.title: Set Up CI/CD Pipeline with GitHub Actions
tasks.description: Automate the build, linting, and testing process for the Android application using a GitHub Actions workflow.
tasks.details:
1. Create a `.github/workflows` directory in the project root. 2. Create a YAML file (e.g., `android-ci.yml`). 3. Define a workflow that triggers on `pull_request` to the `main` or `develop` branch. 4. The workflow should have jobs for: 
   - `setup`: Check out the code, set up Node.js, and install npm dependencies. 
   - `lint`: Run the ESLint checks (`npm run lint`). 
   - `test`: Run the Jest unit tests (`npm run test`). 
   - `build`: Assemble the Android debug build (`cd android && ./gradlew assembleDebug`) to ensure the project builds successfully.
tasks.testStrategy: 1. Create a new branch and open a pull request with code that contains a linting error. Verify that the 'lint' job in the GitHub Actions workflow fails. 2. Fix the linting error and push the change. Verify all jobs in the workflow pass. 3. Check the GitHub Actions tab in the repository to monitor workflow runs and diagnose failures.

subtasks.title: Initialize GitHub Actions Workflow Directory and File
subtasks.description: Create the necessary directory structure `.github/workflows` at the project root and add a new YAML file named `android-ci.yml` to house the continuous integration workflow.
subtasks.details: In the root of the JCar project, create a directory named `.github`. Inside `.github`, create another directory named `workflows`. Finally, create an empty file inside `workflows` named `android-ci.yml`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify that the `.github/workflows/android-ci.yml` file exists in the repository after pushing the changes.

subtasks.title: Define Workflow Triggers and Setup Job
subtasks.description: Configure the `android-ci.yml` workflow to trigger on pull requests to the `main` and `develop` branches. Implement a foundational `setup` job to prepare the environment for subsequent jobs.
subtasks.details: Edit `android-ci.yml`. Define the workflow `name` and the `on` trigger: `pull_request: branches: [ main, develop ]`. Create a `jobs` section with a `setup` job that runs on `ubuntu-latest`. The job steps should include `actions/checkout@v3`, `actions/setup-node@v3` (with caching for npm), and `actions/setup-java@v3` for the Android build. The final step should be `npm install`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Create a pull request and verify that the GitHub Action workflow is triggered and the 'setup' job completes successfully by checking the Actions tab on GitHub.

subtasks.title: Implement Linting Job in Workflow
subtasks.description: Add a `lint` job to the CI pipeline that performs static code analysis on the codebase. This job should depend on the successful completion of the `setup` job.
subtasks.details: In `android-ci.yml`, add a new job named `lint`. Specify `needs: setup` to ensure it runs only after the setup is complete. The job should run on `ubuntu-latest` and reuse the checkout and setup steps or download artifacts from the setup job. The key step is `run: npm run lint`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Open a pull request with a deliberate linting error. Confirm that the `lint` job fails. Fix the error, push the commit, and confirm the `lint` job passes.

subtasks.title: Implement Unit Testing Job in Workflow
subtasks.description: Add a `test` job to the CI pipeline to execute the Jest unit tests. This job should also depend on the `setup` job and can run in parallel with the `lint` job.
subtasks.details: In `android-ci.yml`, add a new job named `test`. Specify `needs: setup`. This job will run on `ubuntu-latest`. The main step for this job will be `run: npm run test` to execute the Jest test suite.
subtasks.testStrategy: Create a pull request with a failing unit test. Verify that the `test` job in the workflow fails as expected. Then, fix the test and push the update to ensure the job passes.

subtasks.title: Implement Android Debug Build Job in Workflow
subtasks.description: Add a `build` job that compiles the Android application to ensure it's in a buildable state. This job is crucial for catching native code or configuration issues early.
subtasks.details: In `android-ci.yml`, add the final job named `build`. It should also have `needs: setup`. The job will run on `ubuntu-latest`. The core steps are to grant execute permissions to the gradlew script (`chmod +x ./android/gradlew`) and then run the build command (`cd ./android && ./gradlew assembleDebug`).
subtasks.testStrategy: Open a pull request with a valid change and verify that the `build` job completes successfully. Check the job logs to ensure the `assembleDebug` task succeeded without errors.

tasks.title: Prepare Android for Production Release
tasks.description: Configure the Android project for a production release, including setting up app signing, enabling code shrinking, and generating a signed Android App Bundle (AAB).
tasks.details: 1. **Keystore**: Generate a private signing key using `keytool`. Store the keystore file and its credentials securely (e.g., using environment variables or a secret manager), not in the repository. 2. **Gradle Configuration**: In `android/app/build.gradle`, create a signing configuration that loads the keystore credentials. Apply this signing config to the `release` build type. 3. **ProGuard/R8**: Enable code shrinking and obfuscation for the release build by setting `minifyEnabled true` in the `release` build type. Add any necessary ProGuard rules to `proguard-rules.pro` to prevent vital code from being stripped. 4. **Generate AAB**: Run the command `./gradlew bundleRelease` from the `android` directory to generate the signed AAB file, which will be located in `android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/`.
tasks.testStrategy: 1. Install the generated release AAB on a physical device to ensure it runs without crashing (which could indicate incorrect ProGuard rules). 2. Test core application flows like login, vehicle browsing, and consultation requests on the release build. 3. Upload the AAB to an internal testing track on the Google Play Console to verify it's correctly signed and configured.

subtasks.title: Generate Android Upload Keystore
subtasks.description: Create a new private signing key using the 'keytool' utility. This key is essential for signing the production release of the Android application and uploading it to the Google Play Store.
subtasks.details: Use the Java `keytool` command-line tool to generate a new `.keystore` file. The command will be similar to `keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore jcar-upload-key.keystore -alias jcar_upload_alias -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000`. Store the generated `jcar-upload-key.keystore` file in a secure location outside of the project's version-controlled directory.
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify that the `jcar-upload-key.keystore` file is successfully created. Document the key alias and passwords in a secure password manager.

subtasks.title: Securely Configure Keystore Credentials
subtasks.description: Store the keystore password, key alias, and key password securely so they can be accessed by the Gradle build process without being committed to version control.
subtasks.details: Create or edit the `android/gradle.properties` file to store the credentials. Add the following properties: `JCAR_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE=path/to/your/jcar-upload-key.keystore`, `JCAR_UPLOAD_KEY_ALIAS=jcar_upload_alias`, `JCAR_UPLOAD_STORE_PASSWORD=your_store_password`, and `JCAR_UPLOAD_KEY_PASSWORD=your_key_password`. Ensure that `gradle.properties` is included in the root `.gitignore` file to prevent it from being committed.
subtasks.testStrategy: Run `git check-ignore android/gradle.properties` to confirm the file is ignored by Git. Verify that Gradle can read these properties by adding a `println` statement in `build.gradle` and running a sync.

subtasks.title: Configure Release Signing in build.gradle
subtasks.description: Modify the `android/app/build.gradle` file to read the secure credentials from `gradle.properties` and apply the signing configuration to the `release` build type.
subtasks.details: In `android/app/build.gradle`, define a `signingConfigs` block for `release` that reads the properties set in the previous task. The configuration should look like: `storeFile file(JCAR_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE)`, `storePassword JCAR_UPLOAD_STORE_PASSWORD`, etc. Then, within the `buildTypes.release` block, set `signingConfig signingConfigs.release`.
subtasks.testStrategy: From the `android` directory, run the `./gradlew :app:signingReport` command. Check the output to ensure the 'release' variant is correctly configured with the 'jcar_upload_alias' and shows no errors.

subtasks.title: Enable Code Shrinking and Obfuscation with R8
subtasks.description: Enable R8 for the release build to reduce app size, remove unused code, and obfuscate class and method names, which enhances security.
subtasks.details: In the `release` build type within `android/app/build.gradle`, set `minifyEnabled true` and `shrinkResources true`. Check for any third-party libraries that might require specific rules to function correctly after minification. Add any necessary `-keep` rules to the `android/app/proguard-rules.pro` file to prevent critical code from being stripped.
subtasks.testStrategy: After generating a release AAB, analyze it using Android Studio's 'Analyze APK' tool to inspect the dex files and confirm that code has been obfuscated. The primary test is to install and run the app to ensure no crashes occur due to incorrect ProGuard rules.

subtasks.title: Generate and Verify Signed Android App Bundle (AAB)
subtasks.description: Execute the final Gradle command to build the signed Android App Bundle (AAB) and perform a verification test on a physical device to ensure its integrity and functionality.
subtasks.details: Navigate to the `android` directory in your terminal and run the command `./gradlew bundleRelease`. This command will compile the code, run R8, and sign the application, producing the final AAB file located at `android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Install the generated `app-release.aab` on a physical Android device, either via `bundletool` or by uploading it to an internal testing track on the Google Play Console. Perform a full smoke test of the application's core features, such as login, vehicle browsing, and consultation requests.

tasks.title: Establish Design System Foundation (Theme)
tasks.description: Create the core theme files for the design system, including color palettes, typography, spacing, border radius, and shadow styles. This will serve as the single source of truth for all UI styling.
tasks.details: Create a `src/theme` directory. Inside, create separate files for each design token category: `colors.js`, `typography.js`, `spacing.js`, `shadows.js`, `borderRadius.js`. Export constants from each file. For example, in `colors.js`: `export const colors = { primary: '#2B4593', success: '#28A745', ... }`. Create a main `index.js` in `src/theme` that exports all tokens as a single theme object. Use React's Context API to provide this theme object to the entire application tree via a `ThemeProvider` component.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit test the theme files to ensure all values from the PRD are correctly defined and exported. Manually review the theme object structure. Integrate the ThemeProvider at the root of the app and verify in a sample component that theme values can be accessed correctly.

subtasks.title: Set Up Theme Directory and File Structure
subtasks.description: Create the necessary directory and empty files for the design system's theme foundation.
subtasks.details: Create a new directory at `src/theme`. Inside this directory, create the following empty files: `colors.js`, `typography.js`, `spacing.js`, `shadows.js`, `borderRadius.js`, and a main `index.js` file for consolidation.
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify that the `src/theme` directory and all specified `.js` files exist in the project structure.

subtasks.title: Define and Export Individual Design Tokens
subtasks.description: Populate each theme file with the specific design tokens (colors, typography, etc.) and export them as constants.
subtasks.details: In each file created in the previous step, define and export the corresponding design tokens. For example, in `src/theme/colors.js`, add `export const colors = { primary: '#2B4593', secondary: '#...', ... }`. Do this for all token files based on the project's PRD.
subtasks.testStrategy: Unit test each file to ensure that it exports a non-empty object with the correct structure and that the values match the design specifications.

subtasks.title: Consolidate All Tokens into a Single Theme Object
subtasks.description: Import all individual token objects into the main theme index file and export them as a single, unified theme object.
subtasks.details: In `src/theme/index.js`, import the constants from `colors.js`, `typography.js`, `spacing.js`, etc. Combine them into a single `theme` object and export it as the default export. Example: `export default { colors, typography, ... }`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Create a test that imports the default export from `src/theme/index.js` and verifies that it is an object containing all the individual token categories as properties (e.g., `theme.colors`, `theme.typography`).

subtasks.title: Create ThemeProvider using React Context API
subtasks.description: Develop a ThemeProvider component that uses React's Context API to make the theme object available to all descendant components.
subtasks.details: Create a new file, for example `src/providers/ThemeProvider.js`. In this file, create a `ThemeContext`. Then, create a `ThemeProvider` component that accepts `children` and provides the consolidated theme object (imported from `src/theme`) through the `ThemeContext.Provider`. Also, create and export a custom hook `useTheme` for easy consumption of the context.
subtasks.testStrategy: Unit test the `ThemeProvider` to ensure it renders its children. Test the `useTheme` hook within a test component wrapped by the provider to verify it returns the correct theme object.

subtasks.title: Integrate ThemeProvider at the Application Root
subtasks.description: Wrap the root component of the application with the new ThemeProvider to make the theme available globally.
subtasks.details: Locate the main entry point of the application (e.g., `App.js`). Import the `ThemeProvider` and wrap the entire application's component tree with it. This will ensure that any component can access the theme via the `useTheme` hook.
subtasks.testStrategy: Manually test the application after integration. Modify a sample component to use the `useTheme` hook and apply a theme style (e.g., `color: theme.colors.primary`). Verify that the style is correctly applied when the app runs.

tasks.title: Develop Unified Button Component
tasks.description: Create a single, reusable Button component that supports all variants (Primary, Secondary, Danger, Success, Text) and states (Default, Hover, Pressed, Disabled) defined in the PRD.
tasks.details: Create a `src/components/Button.js` file. The component should accept props like `variant`, `onPress`, `disabled`, and `title`. Use the theme values from the context for styling. Implement dynamic styling based on the `variant` prop. For example: `const getBackgroundColor = () => { switch(variant) { case 'primary': return theme.colors.primary; case 'danger': return theme.colors.danger; default: return 'transparent'; } };`. Use `Pressable` to handle states like `onPressIn` and `onPressOut` to apply pressed styles (scale transform).
tasks.testStrategy: Use Storybook or a similar tool to visually test all variants and states. Write unit tests using React Native Testing Library to verify that the correct styles are applied for each prop combination and that the `onPress` handler is called when not disabled, and not called when disabled.

subtasks.title: Create Button.js File and Basic Component Structure
subtasks.description: Set up the initial `Button.js` file with a basic functional component structure. It should accept `title` and `onPress` props and render a `Pressable` component containing a `Text` component for the title.
subtasks.details: Create the file `src/components/Button.js`. The component will accept props `(title, onPress, ...rest)`. It will return a `<Pressable onPress={onPress}><Text>{title}</Text></Pressable>`. Apply initial, default styling for the container and text.
subtasks.testStrategy: Manually render the component on a development screen to ensure it displays correctly with a title and is clickable.

subtasks.title: Implement Dynamic Styles for All Button Variants
subtasks.description: Implement the styling logic to support all five variants: Primary, Secondary, Danger, Success, and Text. Styles should be derived from the application's theme context.
subtasks.details: Import and use the application's theme context (e.g., via a `useTheme` hook). Create a style generation function or use a `switch` statement that returns an object with `backgroundColor`, `borderColor`, and `textColor` based on the `variant` prop. Apply these styles to the `Pressable` and `Text` elements.
subtasks.testStrategy: Write a unit test that provides each variant prop to the component and asserts that the returned style object contains the correct theme colors. Visually confirm each variant in the app.

subtasks.title: Implement Styling and Logic for Pressed and Disabled States
subtasks.description: Add visual feedback for the `pressed` state and functional/visual changes for the `disabled` state. The button should provide interaction feedback and appear inactive when disabled.
subtasks.details: Use the `Pressable` component's function-as-a-child for the `style` prop: `style={({ pressed }) => [...]}`. When `pressed`, apply a transform style, e.g., `transform: [{ scale: 0.98 }]`. When the `disabled` prop is true, merge an opacity style (e.g., `{ opacity: 0.5 }`) and ensure the `onPress` handler is blocked.
subtasks.testStrategy: Using React Native Testing Library, simulate a press event and verify the `onPress` callback is not fired when `disabled` is true. Manually press the button to confirm the visual transform and check the disabled appearance.

subtasks.title: Define Prop Types and Finalize Component API
subtasks.description: Formalize the component's public API by adding PropType definitions or TypeScript types for all accepted props, including setting default values.
subtasks.details: Import `PropTypes` from 'prop-types'. Define `Button.propTypes` specifying the type for each prop: `variant` as `oneOf(['primary', 'secondary', 'danger', 'success', 'text'])`, `title` as `string.isRequired`, `onPress` as `func.isRequired`, `disabled` as `bool`. Set default props, e.g., `Button.defaultProps = { variant: 'primary', disabled: false };`.
subtasks.testStrategy: This is a static code quality task. The test is to run the application's linter or type-checker to ensure the definitions are correct and that console warnings are not thrown for valid prop usage.

subtasks.title: Create Storybook for Visual Testing and Documentation
subtasks.description: Develop a Storybook story file for the Button component to visually test all variants and states in an isolated environment, which will also serve as living documentation.
subtasks.details: Create a new file `src/components/Button.stories.js`. Write stories for each `variant`. For each variant, display its default, pressed (via addon), and disabled states to ensure all visual combinations render as expected.
subtasks.testStrategy: The successful creation and rendering of the Storybook stories is the test. Manually navigate through each story in the Storybook UI to visually confirm that all variants and states match the design specifications from the PRD.

tasks.title: Develop Unified Input Field Component
tasks.description: Create a reusable text input component with consistent styling for default, focus, and error states as specified in the PRD.
tasks.details: Create `src/components/InputField.js`. This component will wrap React Native's `TextInput`. It should accept props like `value`, `onChangeText`, `placeholder`, `error` (a string for the error message), etc. Use the `useState` hook to track focus state (`onFocus`, `onBlur`). Apply conditional styling based on focus and the presence of the `error` prop. The error message should be displayed below the input field using the 'Danger' color. All styling (height, padding, border radius, colors) should come from the theme.
tasks.testStrategy: Visually test the component in different states: default, focused, with input text, and with an error message. Write unit tests to check that the border color and style change on focus/blur, and that the error message is rendered correctly when the `error` prop is provided.

subtasks.title: Create Basic InputField Component Structure
subtasks.description: Create the file `src/components/InputField.js` and set up a basic functional component that wraps the React Native `TextInput`. The component should accept and pass through essential props like `value`, `onChangeText`, and `placeholder`.
subtasks.details: Initialize the file at `src/components/InputField.js`. The component should return a `View` containing a `TextInput`. Ensure props like `value`, `onChangeText`, and `placeholder` are correctly passed to the `TextInput` element.
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify that the component renders a text input and that typing in it works as expected.

subtasks.title: Apply Default Styles from Theme
subtasks.description: Integrate the application's theme to apply default styling to the InputField. This includes border radius, background color, padding, text color, and border color for the default (non-focused, no-error) state.
subtasks.details: Use the theme context to access style values. Create a StyleSheet for the component. Apply theme values for `colors.border`, `colors.text`, `spacing.padding`, `borderRadius`, and a fixed height as specified in the PRD.
subtasks.testStrategy: Visually inspect the component to ensure it matches the default state styling defined in the design specifications. Check that all style values are derived from the theme.

subtasks.title: Implement Focus State and Styling
subtasks.description: Use the `useState` hook to track the input's focus state. Implement `onFocus` and `onBlur` handlers to update the state, and apply conditional styling when the input is focused, such as changing the border color.
subtasks.details: Create a state variable `isFocused` initialized to `false`. The `onFocus` prop of `TextInput` should set `isFocused` to `true`, and `onBlur` should set it to `false`. Use this state to conditionally change the `borderColor` to `theme.colors.primary`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Manually test by tapping in and out of the input field. Verify that the border color changes to the primary theme color on focus and reverts to the default color on blur.

subtasks.title: Implement Error State and Message Display
subtasks.description: Handle the `error` prop. When an error string is passed, the input's border color should change to the 'danger' color. The error message itself should be displayed in a `Text` component directly below the input field.
subtasks.details: The component should accept an `error` prop (string). If `error` has a value, override other border color styles with `theme.colors.danger`. Render a `<Text>` component conditionally (`{error && <Text>...}`), styling it with `theme.colors.danger`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Pass a sample error string to the `error` prop and verify that the border becomes red and the error message appears below the input in the correct color.

subtasks.title: Finalize Props and Add Documentation
subtasks.description: Ensure any additional `TextInput` props can be passed to the underlying component using the `...rest` spread operator. Add comprehensive JSDoc comments or PropTypes to document the component's API.
subtasks.details: Modify the component's props to include `{ ...rest }`. Pass this `rest` object directly to the `TextInput` component. Add documentation for primary props like `value`, `onChangeText`, `placeholder`, and `error`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Test passing a standard `TextInput` prop like `keyboardType='numeric'` or `secureTextEntry` to the `InputField` component and verify it functions correctly.

tasks.title: Develop Card and Status Badge Components
tasks.description: Create reusable Card and Badge components. The Card will be a container for content sections, and the Badge will be used to display status labels like '대기중', '승인', etc.
tasks.details: For `src/components/Card.js`, create a `View` with styles defined by the PRD (background, border radius, padding, shadow). It should accept `children` to render any content inside. For `src/components/Badge.js`, the component should take a `status` prop ('waiting', 'approved', 'rejected', 'completed'). Based on the status, it should apply the corresponding semantic color from the theme (Warning for waiting, Success for approved, etc.) for its background. All styling should be derived from the theme.
tasks.testStrategy: Visually test the Card component with various child elements to ensure padding and shadow are correct. For the Badge, create a Storybook story that displays all status variants to confirm correct color mapping and styling. Unit test the Badge to ensure the `status` prop correctly maps to the theme color.

subtasks.title: Create Card.js Component File and Basic Structure
subtasks.description: Initialize the `Card.js` file within `src/components/`. Set up a basic React Native functional component that accepts and renders `children` props within a `View`.
subtasks.details: Create the file at `src/components/Card.js`. The component should be a simple functional component that receives `children` and an optional `style` prop and renders them inside a `View`. Example: `const Card = ({ children, style }) => <View style={[styles.container, style]}>{children}</View>;`
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify the file is created and the component can render simple text passed as a child element without crashing.

subtasks.title: Apply Theme-Based Styling to the Card Component
subtasks.description: Enhance the `Card` component by applying styles for background color, border radius, padding, and shadow. These styles must be derived from the application's theme.
subtasks.details: Access the theme context to retrieve styling values. Apply a background color (e.g., `theme.colors.surface`), padding (e.g., `theme.spacing.m`), and border radius (e.g., `theme.radii.m`). Implement platform-specific shadow for iOS and elevation for Android.
subtasks.testStrategy: Visually test the component on a screen with a different background color to confirm shadow and padding are correctly applied. Render various child elements inside to test content layout.

subtasks.title: Create Badge.js Component File and Define Prop Interface
subtasks.description: Create the `src/components/Badge.js` file. Set up a functional component that accepts a `status` prop with defined possible values ('waiting', 'approved', 'rejected', 'completed') and renders a `View` containing a `Text` element.
subtasks.details: Create the file `src/components/Badge.js`. The component signature should be `const Badge = ({ status }) => { ... };`. It should be prepared to handle dynamic styling and text content based on the `status` prop.
subtasks.testStrategy: Confirm the file is created and the component renders a default state without errors when passed a valid status prop.

subtasks.title: Implement Dynamic Styling and Text Mapping for Badge
subtasks.description: Implement the core logic for the `Badge` component. This includes mapping the `status` prop to a specific background color from the theme and a corresponding Korean text label (e.g., 'waiting' -> '대기중').
subtasks.details: Create a helper function or a configuration object to map each status to its theme color and text. For example: `const config = { waiting: { color: theme.colors.warning, text: '대기중' }, approved: { color: theme.colors.success, text: '승인' } };`. Use this config to dynamically set the `backgroundColor` of the `View` and the content of the `Text` component.
subtasks.testStrategy: Write a unit test for the mapping logic to ensure each status string input returns the correct color value and text string output.

subtasks.title: Finalize Badge Styling and Document with Storybook
subtasks.description: Add final styling touches to the Badge, such as padding, border radius, and text styling. Create a Storybook story to display all variants of the Badge, and an example of the Card containing content.
subtasks.details: In `Badge.js`, apply styles from the theme for horizontal/vertical padding, border-radius, and text color/font size to ensure readability and a polished look. Create `Badge.stories.js` to render a list of all badge variants ('waiting', 'approved', 'rejected', 'completed') for visual regression testing.
subtasks.testStrategy: Use Storybook to visually inspect all Badge variants to confirm correct color mapping, text labels, and padding. Also, verify that the Card component renders correctly with a Badge and other content inside.

tasks.title: Refactor Login and Sign-up Screens
tasks.description: Apply the new design system to the Login and Sign-up screens, replacing existing elements with the new unified Button and Input Field components and adjusting layout spacing.
tasks.details: Navigate to the authentication screen files. Replace all `<Button>` and `<TextInput>` instances with the new `<Button>` and `<InputField>` components. Use the 'primary' variant for the main action button and 'text' variant for links like '비밀번호 찾기'. Remove any hardcoded style values and use spacing tokens from the theme for margins and paddings between the logo, input fields, and buttons as per the PRD.
tasks.testStrategy: Perform visual regression testing to compare the old screens with the newly styled ones. Manually test the login and sign-up flows to ensure functionality is unchanged. Check that focus, error, and button press states work as expected.

subtasks.title: Refactor Input Fields and Layout on Login Screen
subtasks.description: Navigate to the Login screen file. Replace all existing `TextInput` components with the new, unified `InputField` component from the design system. Adjust the layout by removing hardcoded styles and applying spacing tokens from the theme for consistent margins and padding between the logo, inputs, and other elements.
subtasks.details: Identify the main login screen file, likely located at `src/screens/auth/LoginScreen.tsx`. Import the new `InputField` component. Systematically replace each `TextInput` for email and password. Utilize the theme provider hook (e.g., `useTheme`) to access spacing tokens (`theme.spacing.medium`, etc.) and apply them via the style prop for vertical spacing.
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify that the `InputField` components render correctly. Check that placeholder text is visible and that users can type into the fields. Confirm that layout spacing matches the new design specifications.

subtasks.title: Refactor Buttons on Login Screen
subtasks.description: In the Login screen file, replace the existing primary action button and any text-based navigation links with the new unified `Button` component, using the appropriate variants.
subtasks.details: In `src/screens/auth/LoginScreen.tsx`, import the new `Button` component. Replace the main login submission button with `<Button variant="primary" title="로그인">`. Replace text links like '비밀번호 찾기' and '회원가입' with `<Button variant="text" title="비밀번호 찾기">`. Ensure all `onPress` handlers are correctly reassigned to the new components.
subtasks.testStrategy: Manually test that the primary button is tappable and triggers the login function. Verify that the text buttons navigate to the correct screens (Forgot Password, Sign-up). Check that the button styles match the 'primary' and 'text' variants from the design system.

subtasks.title: Refactor Input Fields and Layout on Sign-up Screen
subtasks.description: Navigate to the Sign-up screen file. Replace all `TextInput` components with the new `InputField` component and apply theme spacing tokens to standardize the layout, similar to the Login screen.
subtasks.details: Locate the sign-up screen file, likely at `src/screens/auth/SignUpScreen.tsx`. Import the `InputField` component. Replace all text inputs (e.g., email, password, confirm password, name) with the new component. Apply spacing tokens from the theme to ensure consistent vertical rhythm between form elements.
subtasks.testStrategy: Confirm all `InputField` components render correctly on the Sign-up screen. Test user input in all fields. Verify the layout is consistent with the refactored Login screen and meets PRD specifications.

subtasks.title: Refactor Buttons on Sign-up Screen
subtasks.description: In the Sign-up screen file, replace the existing primary action button and text links with the new `Button` component, applying the correct variants.
subtasks.details: In `src/screens/auth/SignUpScreen.tsx`, import the `Button` component. Replace the main registration button with `<Button variant="primary" title="회원가입">`. Convert the '이미 계정이 있나요? 로그인' link to use the `<Button variant="text">`. Re-connect the `onPress` handlers to the new components.
subtasks.testStrategy: Test that the primary 'Sign-up' button triggers the registration logic. Verify the 'Login' text button navigates back to the Login screen. Ensure button styles are consistent with the design system.

subtasks.title: Final Review and Functional Testing of Auth Flow
subtasks.description: Perform a comprehensive visual review and functional test of the entire authentication flow, covering both the Login and Sign-up screens, to ensure functionality is preserved and styling is consistent.
subtasks.details: Manually navigate between the Login and Sign-up screens. Test the complete sign-up process with valid and invalid data to check error states. Test the login process with correct and incorrect credentials. Perform a visual comparison of both screens against the PRD mockups to catch any inconsistencies in layout, spacing, or component styling.
subtasks.testStrategy: Execute a full end-to-end test case for user registration and another for user login. Perform visual regression testing by comparing screenshots of the old and new screens. Verify that focus states, error messages, and button press states work as expected.

tasks.title: Refactor Vehicle List and Detail Screens
tasks.description: Update the Vehicle List and Detail screens using the new design system components, including Card, Badge, and standardized typography and layout.
tasks.details: On the Vehicle List screen, wrap each list item in the new `<Card>` component. Use theme spacing for gaps between cards. Re-style the header according to the PRD. Inside the card, use the `<Badge>` for vehicle type and apply H3/Body typography from the theme. On the Vehicle Detail screen, structure content into sections with H4 titles. Use the theme for padding and spacing. Implement the fixed bottom action button using the primary `<Button>` component.
tasks.testStrategy: Manually navigate through the vehicle list and tap into detail pages. Verify that all elements use the new components and theme styles. Check for layout consistency across different list items. Ensure the bottom action button on the detail screen is fixed and functional.

subtasks.title: Refactor VehicleListItem to use Card and Badge Components
subtasks.description: Update the individual item component rendered in the vehicle list to use the new <Card> as its root element. Inside the card, replace existing elements with <Badge> for the vehicle type and apply H3/Body typography from the theme for other text.
subtasks.details: Locate the component used for rendering each vehicle in the FlatList on the Vehicle List Screen. Replace the main container View with the <Card> component. Import and use the <Badge> component for vehicle status/type. Apply theme.typography.h3 and theme.typography.body styles to the relevant <Text> components.
subtasks.testStrategy: Visually inspect the new list item component in a Storybook or on the list screen to ensure it matches the PRD design. Verify correct props are passed to Card and Badge.

subtasks.title: Update Vehicle List Screen Layout and Header
subtasks.description: Adjust the main FlatList on the Vehicle List screen to use theme spacing for the gap between the new Card items. Restyle the screen's header to match the new design system specifications.
subtasks.details: In the VehicleListScreen file, modify the FlatList props. Use ItemSeparatorComponent or contentContainerStyle with a gap property set from the theme (e.g., theme.spacing.m). Update the header component or options in the navigation stack to apply the new typography and layout.
subtasks.testStrategy: Scroll through the vehicle list to confirm consistent spacing between all items. Check that the header style is correctly applied and consistent with other refactored screens.

subtasks.title: Restructure Vehicle Detail Screen with Theme Spacing and Typography
subtasks.description: Refactor the layout of the Vehicle Detail screen to organize content into logical sections. Apply H4 typography for section titles and use theme-defined padding and spacing for all elements.
subtasks.details: Open the VehicleDetailScreen file. Wrap content sections in <View> containers. Apply padding to the main screen container using theme.spacing.l. For each section, add a <Text> component with theme.typography.h4 style for the title. Ensure all margins and paddings use the theme's spacing tokens.
subtasks.testStrategy: Visually verify the detail screen's layout against the design mockups. Check that all spacing is consistent and typography is correctly applied to section headers and body text.

subtasks.title: Implement Fixed Bottom Action Button on Vehicle Detail Screen
subtasks.description: Add a primary <Button> component to the Vehicle Detail screen that is fixed to the bottom of the viewport for the main call-to-action, such as '상담 신청'.
subtasks.details: In VehicleDetailScreen, import the new <Button> component. Place it inside a View with absolute positioning (position: 'absolute', bottom: 0, left: 0, right: 0) and appropriate padding from the theme. Set the variant to 'primary' and pass the correct onPress handler.
subtasks.testStrategy: Navigate to the detail screen and confirm the button is visible and fixed at the bottom. Scroll the content to ensure the button remains in place. Tap the button to verify its action is triggered.

subtasks.title: Verify Navigation and Perform Final Visual Review
subtasks.description: Ensure the navigation from the refactored Vehicle List screen to the refactored Vehicle Detail screen is working correctly. Conduct a final visual review of both screens to catch any inconsistencies.
subtasks.details: Test the onPress handler on the new <Card> component in the vehicle list to ensure it navigates with the correct vehicleId. Review both screens on different device sizes if possible. Clean up any unused styles or imports from the old implementation.
subtasks.testStrategy: Perform an end-to-end test: start on the list screen, scroll, tap a vehicle card, view the detail screen, scroll, and interact with the bottom button. Compare both screens side-by-side with the PRD.

tasks.title: Implement Standardized Navigation Headers and Tab Bar
tasks.description: Apply a consistent design to the global navigation header and bottom tab bar across the application, using the styles defined in the PRD.
tasks.details: This task likely involves configuring the navigation library (e.g., React Navigation). Define a common `headerStyle` object using theme colors (`primary` for background, `white` for text) and apply it as a default screen option. For the tab bar, configure `tabBarOptions` or `tabBarStyle` to set the background, height, and active/inactive tint colors using the theme. The active tab's top border can be implemented using a custom tab bar component if the library doesn't support it directly.
tasks.testStrategy: Navigate through all major sections of the app and verify that the header and tab bar have a consistent appearance. Check that the active tab state (color, border) is correctly displayed on each screen.

subtasks.title: Define Centralized Navigation Style Constants
subtasks.description: Create a dedicated file to define and export style objects for the global header and tab bar, pulling values from the application's theme file.
subtasks.details: Create a new file at `src/navigation/navigationStyles.js`. In this file, import the application's theme object. Export a `defaultHeaderOptions` object containing `headerStyle`, `headerTintColor`, and `headerTitleStyle`. Also, export a `defaultTabBarOptions` object containing `tabBarStyle`, `tabBarActiveTintColor`, and `tabBarInactiveTintColor`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Review the created file to ensure it correctly imports theme colors and exports the style configuration objects for both header and tab bar.

subtasks.title: Apply Standardized Styles to the Global Header
subtasks.description: Update the root Stack Navigator configuration to import and apply the centralized header style object as its default `screenOptions`.
subtasks.details: Locate the primary `StackNavigator` component in the application, likely in `src/navigation/AppNavigator.js`. Import the `defaultHeaderOptions` object from `navigationStyles.js` and spread it into the `screenOptions` prop of the `Stack.Navigator` component to apply the style to all screens within that stack.
subtasks.testStrategy: Run the app and observe that all screens governed by the main stack navigator now share the same header background color, title color, and font style.

subtasks.title: Apply Standardized Styles to the Bottom Tab Bar
subtasks.description: Configure the main BottomTabNavigator to use the centralized tab bar style object for its background, height, and active/inactive icon and label colors.
subtasks.details: Find the `BottomTabNavigator` component. Import the `defaultTabBarOptions` from `navigationStyles.js`. Apply these options to the `screenOptions` prop of the `Tab.Navigator`. This will set the `tabBarStyle`, `tabBarActiveTintColor`, and `tabBarInactiveTintColor` for all tabs.
subtasks.testStrategy: Launch the application and verify the bottom tab bar's background color is correct. Tap between different tabs to confirm that the active and inactive tint colors for icons and labels match the defined styles.

subtasks.title: Implement Active Tab Top Border Indicator
subtasks.description: Implement the visual indicator (a colored top border) for the currently active tab in the bottom tab bar as specified in the PRD.
subtasks.details: Since React Navigation's default tab bar doesn't directly support a top border on the active item, update the `tabBarIcon` function for each `Tab.Screen`. The function should return a `View` that wraps the icon. This `View` will conditionally apply a `borderTopWidth` and `borderTopColor` style when its `focused` prop is true.
subtasks.testStrategy: Navigate between tabs and confirm that only the currently active tab icon displays a top border with the correct color and thickness. Ensure the border does not appear on inactive tabs.

subtasks.title: Full App Navigation Style Verification and Cleanup
subtasks.description: Perform a comprehensive review of the entire application to ensure the new navigation styles are applied consistently and remove any old, screen-specific header or tab bar style overrides.
subtasks.details: Manually navigate to every screen, including nested screens within stacks. Identify any screens that still have local `options` prop styling for the header that conflicts with the new global style. Remove these local overrides unless they are intentionally different. Ensure a consistent user experience across the app.
subtasks.testStrategy: Test on both iOS and Android. Create a checklist of all screens. Go through the checklist, verifying header and tab bar appearance on each screen. Confirm that no legacy styling remains.

tasks.title: Create Interaction State Components (Loading, Empty, Error)
tasks.description: Develop reusable components for displaying global loading spinners, skeleton loaders for lists, and full-page empty/error states.
tasks.details: 1. `GlobalLoader`: A modal overlay with a semi-transparent background and an `ActivityIndicator` using the theme's primary color. 2. `SkeletonLoader`: A component that mimics the layout of a `<Card>` but with placeholder shapes and a shimmering animation. 3. `StateScreen`: A generic component accepting `icon`, `title`, `message`, and `onRetry` props to display consistent empty or error screens. It should use the secondary `<Button>` for the retry action.
tasks.testStrategy: Use Storybook to visually test each state component. Unit test the `StateScreen` to ensure props are rendered correctly and the `onRetry` callback is fired. Manually trigger these states in the app (e.g., by simulating a network delay or error) to see them in context.

subtasks.title: Implement the GlobalLoader Component
subtasks.description: Create a reusable full-screen modal component that displays a loading indicator to block UI interactions during global asynchronous operations.
subtasks.details: Create a new component at `src/components/common/GlobalLoader.tsx`. Utilize React Native's `Modal` component with a semi-transparent background overlay. Center an `ActivityIndicator` component within the modal and configure it to use the primary color from the application's theme.
subtasks.testStrategy: Create a Storybook story to visually test the component in isolation. Verify the modal's transparency, the loader's color, and its centered position on the screen.

subtasks.title: Develop the SkeletonLoader Component
subtasks.description: Build a skeleton loader that mimics the layout and structure of a standard Card component, providing a placeholder UI with a shimmering animation while content is loading.
subtasks.details: Create the component at `src/components/common/SkeletonLoader.tsx`. Use a library like `react-native-skeleton-placeholder` to define shapes (e.g., rectangles for images, lines for text) that match the card layout. Ensure the shimmering animation is smooth and performant.
subtasks.testStrategy: Add a Storybook story for the `SkeletonLoader` to visually confirm that the layout correctly mimics a card and that the shimmering animation works as expected on both iOS and Android.

subtasks.title: Create the Generic StateScreen Component
subtasks.description: Develop a versatile, full-page component for displaying empty data states or error messages, complete with an optional retry action.
subtasks.details: Create the file `src/components/common/StateScreen.tsx`. The component must accept `icon`, `title`, `message`, and an optional `onRetry` function as props. If the `onRetry` prop is provided, a secondary-styled `Button` should be rendered that triggers the callback when pressed.
subtasks.testStrategy: Write unit tests using Jest and React Native Testing Library to assert that all props are rendered correctly and that the `onRetry` function is called on button press. Create multiple stories in Storybook to represent different use cases (e.g., an empty state, an error state with a retry button).

subtasks.title: Implement a LoadingContext for Global State Management
subtasks.description: Establish a React Context to manage the visibility of the GlobalLoader, allowing any component in the app to toggle the loader without prop drilling.
subtasks.details: Create a new context at `src/context/LoadingContext.tsx`. The context provider should manage a boolean state for the loader's visibility and render the `GlobalLoader` component. Expose `showLoader` and `hideLoader` functions via a custom hook (e.g., `useLoading`). Wrap the root component in `App.tsx` with this provider.
subtasks.testStrategy: Manually test on a development screen by adding two buttons. One button will call `showLoader()` and the other will call `hideLoader()`. Verify the global loader appears and disappears as expected.

subtasks.title: Integrate All State Components into Storybook
subtasks.description: Create Storybook stories for all three new components (`GlobalLoader`, `SkeletonLoader`, `StateScreen`) to ensure they can be developed and reviewed in isolation.
subtasks.details: In the project's stories directory, create `GlobalLoader.stories.tsx`, `SkeletonLoader.stories.tsx`, and `StateScreen.stories.tsx`. For `StateScreen`, define multiple named exports to showcase its different configurations (e.g., 'EmptyState', 'ErrorWithRetry').
subtasks.testStrategy: Run the Storybook instance and navigate to each new story. Verify that each component and its variations render correctly and are interactive where applicable (e.g., the retry button in `StateScreen`).

tasks.title: Implement Global Toast Message System
tasks.description: Set up a global system to display toast messages for success, error, and info feedback, accessible from anywhere in the app.
tasks.details: Use a library like `react-native-toast-message` or build a custom solution using a global context provider. Create a `ToastProvider` at the app's root. Define custom toast types ('success', 'danger', 'info') that map to the semantic colors in the theme. Expose a hook like `useToast()` which provides functions (`toast.showSuccess(message)`, `toast.showError(message)`) to trigger toasts from any component.
tasks.testStrategy: Create a test screen with buttons to trigger each type of toast message. Verify that they appear with the correct background color, text color, and content, and that they disappear automatically after a few seconds. Ensure the toast can be triggered from various places in the component tree.

subtasks.title: Install and Configure react-native-toast-message
subtasks.description: Add the `react-native-toast-message` library to the project dependencies and perform any necessary native configuration for both iOS and Android platforms.
subtasks.details: Run `npm install react-native-toast-message` or `yarn add react-native-toast-message`. Follow the library's documentation to add required code to `MainActivity.java` for Android and potentially `AppDelegate.m` for iOS if needed. Ensure the project builds successfully after installation.
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify the app builds without errors on both iOS and Android simulators after adding the library.

subtasks.title: Define Custom Toast Components and Configuration
subtasks.description: Create custom React components for 'success', 'danger', and 'info' toast types. These components will use the semantic colors defined in the application's theme.
subtasks.details: Create a `toastConfig.js` file. In this file, import the `BaseToast` from the library and extend it to create custom components. For each type ('success', 'danger', 'info'), set the `style` and `text1Style` properties using the corresponding colors from the theme (e.g., `theme.colors.semantic.success`).
subtasks.testStrategy: Create Storybook stories for each custom toast component to visually inspect their appearance and ensure they render correctly with different message lengths, using the correct theme colors.

subtasks.title: Integrate Toast Provider at App Root
subtasks.description: Wrap the root of the application with the Toast provider component to make it available globally across all screens.
subtasks.details: In the main `App.tsx` file, import the `Toast` component from `react-native-toast-message` and the custom configuration from `toastConfig.js`. Render `<Toast config={toastConfig} />` as the last child within the root view or fragment, ensuring it overlays all other content.
subtasks.testStrategy: After adding the provider, manually trigger a basic toast from a temporary button on the home screen to confirm the provider is set up correctly and the toast appears on screen.

subtasks.title: Create a `useToast` Hook for Global Access
subtasks.description: Develop a custom hook named `useToast` that encapsulates the logic for showing different types of toasts, providing a clean and reusable API.
subtasks.details: Create a new file `src/hooks/useToast.ts`. This hook will import the `Toast` API from the library. It should return an object with methods like `showSuccess(message, options)`, `showError(message, options)`, and `showInfo(message, options)`. Each method will call `Toast.show()` with the corresponding `type` ('success', 'danger', 'info') and the passed message.
subtasks.testStrategy: Unit test the `useToast` hook. Mock the `react-native-toast-message` library and verify that calling `showSuccess('Test')` on the hook's return value calls the underlying `Toast.show` method with the correct parameters (`{ type: 'success', text1: 'Test' }`).

subtasks.title: Implement a Test Screen and Verify All Toast Types
subtasks.description: Create or modify a development/test screen with buttons to trigger each type of toast message using the `useToast` hook.
subtasks.details: Add a new screen or a section in an existing developer settings screen. Add three buttons: 'Show Success', 'Show Error', and 'Show Info'. In the component, call the `useToast()` hook and link each button's `onPress` to the corresponding function (`showSuccess`, `showError`, `showInfo`) with a sample message.
subtasks.testStrategy: Manually press each button on the test screen. Verify that the correct toast appears with the right background color and text. Check that it disappears automatically. Confirm that toasts can be triggered multiple times and queue correctly.

subtasks.title: Refactor MyPage User Info Section with Card Component

subtasks.title: Implement Styled Tab Bar for Admin Screens

subtasks.details: In the relevant Admin screen file (e.g., 'VehicleApprovalScreen.js'), modify the list rendering logic. Each item in the FlatList or map should be wrapped in a <Card>. Use the <Badge> component to display item status (e.g., 'Pending', 'Approved').

subtasks.title: Replace Admin Action Buttons with New Component Variants

tasks.title: Resolve Dependabot Security Alerts
tasks.description: Review and resolve 8 security vulnerabilities (2 high, 3 moderate, 3 low) reported by GitHub Dependabot by updating npm packages and ensuring application stability.
tasks.details:
This task addresses security vulnerabilities identified in project dependencies. First, review all open alerts at https://github.com/E01x001/JCar/security/dependabot. Create a dedicated branch for this work (e.g., `fix/dependabot-vulns`). Use `npm audit` to get a detailed report locally. Address the vulnerabilities starting with the 'high' severity alerts, then 'moderate', and finally 'low'. Update packages individually or in small, logical groups using `npm install <package-name>@latest`. After each update, run `npm install` to regenerate the `package-lock.json` file. For any major version updates, consult the package's release notes for potential breaking changes. IMPORTANT: This is a special maintenance task and should not be completed until explicitly requested by the project lead.
